course: I believe that the biggest problem about this lecture is grading. By this, I don't mean the way how instructor grades, rather, it's the very grading catalogue of this course. According to this catalogue, if you finish the semester with a 86 out of 100, you'll get a B, which is stated as "very good". But consider this: If I graduate with a transcript composed of full of B's and if I say to the job interviewer that I'm very good at everything, would this make any sense? I think that the answer is a huge "no" but here's the way it is, therefore I believe that this point deserves a reconsideration from the executives. In fact, the biggest problem with grading is not that it lowers the GPA etc. but it directly hurts the actual objective of this course. I'll directly quote from the page which explains the aim/objective of this lecture: "General humanities courses provide an important opportunity for students to prepare for truly university level thinking by teaching them certain analytic and critical reading skills, and by teaching them to question texts, professors, and one another.". I genuinely believe that these attributes are much more important than any technical information that we will gain about our own departments, yet, I just can't help but to ask this question: Do I really learn how to distinguish useful evidences from irrelevant information to defend/refute something or do I just aim for getting away with a sufficient grade? I was lucky enough to concentrate on the former one since I had the opportunity to use "Pass/Fail" option and just didn't care about my GPA but this won't be the case for everyone. In short, I believe that Dr. Kimball makes an incredible job by making an effort to every single lecture and it's quite obvious to realize that but this "harsh" grading catalogue harms the actual purpose of this course. Thus, I believe that the executives should at least think about this for a moment.
